record.title: Anthropic publishes detailed recommendations for designing and reporting AI safety evaluations
record.summary: Anthropic’s 13 November 2026 engineering post presents recommendations for designing, running and reporting AI safety evaluations. It emphasizes matching the design to the question, measuring harm-related behavior rather than refusal alone, testing multi-turn and realistic scenarios, validating graders against independent human labels, preregistering analyses, and reporting uncertainty and configuration. The post reports that appropriate-response rate in one Claude Fable 5.1 multi-turn suicide and self-harm evaluation was 60% (±14%) on the API without a system prompt and 94% (±7%) on claude.ai with the product system prompt. Anthropic’s later official system card reproduces those rates and uncertainty. These are first-party results; the comparison does not isolate one mitigation, and the review did not establish external generalization.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Anthropic published a detailed engineering post recommending that safety evaluations define the construct they measure, use realistic multi-turn cases where relevant, validate graders against human labels, preregister analyses, report uncertainty and document configurations. The publication and the recommendations it contains are directly inspectable; their effectiveness outside Anthropic is not demonstrated.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Anthropic reports that, in a multi-turn suicide and self-harm evaluation for Claude Fable 5.1, appropriate-response rate was 60% (±14%) on the API without a system prompt and 94% (±7%) on claude.ai with the product system prompt. The result is source-reported; it does not isolate the causal contribution of one system-prompt mitigation or establish generalization.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected post does not establish that the recommendations improve safety-evaluation validity or decision quality at external laboratories, nor that the reported 34-percentage-point difference generalizes to other models, domains or evaluation designs.

evidence_gaps.description: The post’s evaluation-design recommendations and the API/claude.ai example have not been independently assessed for transfer to other labs, models or domains.

The official later system card reports ±14% and ±7% uncertainty for the example, but no sample size; the API without a system prompt and claude.ai with a production prompt are different configurations, so the effect of one intervention cannot be isolated.

brief.importance_rationale: If the recommendations improve safety-evaluation validity when used by other teams, they could change how labs compare models and make deployment decisions. This is a meaningful methodological contribution, while the reported API/product difference is one first-party example and external effectiveness is not established.
limitations: All substantive recommendations and reported internal results come from one first-party Anthropic post; no external adoption or outcome study was inspected.
The post attributes the 60% to 94% change to a system-prompt instruction and other targeted mitigations, so the effect cannot be assigned to one intervention.
The article does not give the sample size for the 60% versus 94% example; Anthropic’s later official system card reports uncertainty of ±14% and ±7%, respectively.
The post displays a publication date of 13 November 2026 but no exact time; this record does not establish that the item meets the rolling 36-hour newsroom freshness threshold.
The API-without-system-prompt and claude.ai-with-product-system-prompt comparison changes multiple configuration elements, so the effect cannot be attributed to one mitigation.
brief.summary: Anthropic’s 13 November 2026 engineering post presents recommendations for designing, running and reporting AI safety evaluations. It emphasizes matching the design to the question, measuring harm-related behavior rather than refusal alone, testing multi-turn and realistic scenarios, validating graders against independent human labels, preregistering analyses, and reporting uncertainty and configuration. The post reports that appropriate-response rate in one Claude Fable 5.1 multi-turn suicide and self-harm evaluation was 60% (±14%) on the API without a system prompt and 94% (±7%) on claude.ai with the product system prompt. technical.claimed_result: Anthropic reports appropriate-response rates of 60% (±14%) on the API without a system prompt and 94% (±7%) on claude.ai with the product system prompt for Claude Fable 5.1 in a multi-turn suicide and self-harm evaluation.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official post and its recommendations are directly inspectable. The reported rates and the effectiveness or transfer of the recommendations remain first-party claims, not independently demonstrated findings.
technical.mechanism: The post recommends separating capability success from safety behavior, defining domain-specific standards of an appropriate response, using multi-turn scenario generation for context-dependent risks, testing graders and harnesses for bias and failure, preregistering analyses, and documenting model and product configuration.
technical.regime: Anthropic’s own safety-evaluation practice as described in an engineering post and its later official system card. The numeric example concerns Claude Fable 5.1 in a multi-turn suicide and self-harm evaluation, comparing API without a system prompt with claude.ai using its production system prompt.
technical.reproducibility: The later official system card reproduces the two reported rates and uncertainty. The linked Fable 5.1 system card could not be fetched due to its size; sample size and single-intervention attribution remain unresolved. No independent replication was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The post offers no external benchmark or independent comparison of its recommendations. For its Fable 5.1 example, it compares API with claude.ai after targeted system-prompt changes and other mitigations; this is a configuration comparison, not an isolated model or single-intervention baseline.

brief.title: Anthropic publishes detailed recommendations for designing and reporting AI safety evaluations
brief.why_it_matters: Safety evaluations inform model release, safeguard and training decisions, so construct validity, grader reliability and configuration comparability can materially affect conclusions. The post gives practitioners a concrete framework and reports a large API/product configuration difference in one self-harm evaluation. Its practical value is methodological; the reported example is first-party and under-specified here, and the guidance’s external effectiveness has not been tested in this review.
